items.headline: No provision in Forest Rights Act to obtain gram sabha consent for projects: Ministry
items.gist: The Tribal Affairs Ministry told the Power Ministry on August 31 that the 2006 FRA has "no provision for obtaining consent of the Gram Sabha for forest clearance" and such matters do not fall under its purview, though Forest Conservation Act guidelines require completing FRA processes and gram sabha NOCs before diverting forest land; the exchange followed a Parliamentary panel report citing 106-month average forest clearance delays for NHPC projects such as Teesta-IV HEP.

items.headline: Road map ready to make India drug-free by 2029, says Shah
items.gist: Union Home Minister Amit Shah said in Panaji on Sunday that the government has prepared a road map to make India drug-free by 2029, asserting a drug-free youth population would lead to Viksit Bharat by 2047, after chairing a high-level narcotics meeting with Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant. He said the Centre's coordinated nationwide strategy targets the entire narcotics network from trafficking to financing while focusing on rehabilitation, through the four-tier NCORD mechanism created in 2019, dedicated Anti-Narcotics Task Forces in all States and Union Territories, a 2019 Joint Coordination Committee, a strengthened NCB, and the 1933 MANAS helpline for persons with drug addiction.

items.headline: As yoga and Ayurveda become part of India's global health diplomacy, experts press for credible standards
items.gist: Yoga and Ayurveda are increasingly part of India's global health and diplomatic strategy, with trade agreements including the India-Oman CEPA operationalised in June 2026, the India-New Zealand FTA and the India-EU FTA signed in January 2026 easing licensing, standards and AYUSH practitioner mobility. Ministry of AYUSH officials said foreign medical arrivals rose from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.44 lakh in 2024—though that figure covers overall foreign medical arrivals, not AYUSH patients specifically—and that 3,375 foreign nationals travelled on AYUSH or e-AYUSH visas between January 2023 and December 2025; experts warn credible standards, evidence, regulation and practitioner quality are needed for success in regulated global healthcare markets.

items.headline: All the hard work is paying off, says Rudrankksh as he gears up for Asiad
items.gist: Rudrankksh Balasaheb Patil, 22, heading to his second Asian Games in Nagoya from September 14 after a preparatory camp in Bhopal, will compete in 10m air rifle and 50m 3 Position and said all his hard work is paying off. The only Indian male shooter in two events said his aim is gold, that he missed a 10m medal by the barest margins last time, and that he is now more in control of body and mind between events.

items.headline: Netanyahu orders West Bank settler outposts to be removed
items.gist: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered unauthorized settler outposts in the West Bank to be dismantled, two people familiar with the matter said on Sunday, amid US pressure to crack down on settler attacks on Palestinians. The order applies to outposts established by settlers without official Israeli authorisation, typically prefabricated caravans housing a small number of settlers; it was not immediately clear when the operation would begin.

Afghanistan's poorly regulated mining industry sees frequent fatal accidents in coal, marble, mineral, gold and precious-stone operations.

items.headline: Over 140 killed in Yemen clashes
items.gist: Fighting between Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in southwest Yemen killed more than 140 combatants between midday Saturday and early Sunday, military sources said. Two Saudi-backed government officials told AFP that 84 of their troops were killed, mostly in missile attacks, while four Houthi military sources said 57 rebel fighters were killed in the same period.

items.headline: Jakarta airport suspends ops
items.gist: About 170,000 passengers were stranded on Sunday as Indonesia shuttered Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and seven others, cancelling hundreds of flights after Mount Anak Krakatoa spewed volcanic ash and lava from more than 150 kilometres away. The volcano erupted on Saturday with lava fountains and booming sounds heard hundreds of kilometres away, and two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday; ash in surrounding airspace prompted authorities to suspend operations from 1:30 am to 5:30 am Sunday.

items.headline: Iran threatens greater force if US launches more attacks
items.gist: Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, acting as chief negotiator, threatened a faster, more intense and more painful response to any further US attacks after Tehran targeted American warships in the latest round of clashes amid a six-month war deadlock. US Central Command said Iran unsuccessfully fired at an aircraft carrier and a destroyer on Saturday, while the IRGC claimed the warships retreated after suffering damage; CENTCOM said it then struck three oil tankers linked to the Iranian Guards—M/T Downy off Kharg Island, M/T Stark 1 near Jask, and M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman.

items.headline: B'desh: Hindu rights leader gets bail; release unlikely
items.gist: Bangladesh's High Court on Sunday granted bail to jailed Hindu rights leader Chinmoy Krishna Das in two more vandalism and obstruction cases, but his release remains unlikely as he faces charges in other cases. Das was arrested in November 2024 on sedition charges for allegedly disrespecting the national flag and was subsequently booked in several additional cases including murder, attempted murder and vandalism; he now has High Court bail in four of six criminal cases but will not be released immediately because of the remaining charges.

items.headline: Iran to tackle economic issues amid rising tensions
items.gist: Iran said it will step up efforts to tackle problems created by US sanctions crippling its economy, while a senior official warned of a "painful response" if it comes under further attack, six months after US-Israeli strikes and with a preliminary June ceasefire accord unravelled. After tit-for-tat strikes resumed in September, US Central Command said it hit three Iranian tankers on Saturday following IRGC ballistic missile attacks on two US Navy ships; Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said on Sunday that rules of the game in the war against Iran have changed and any attack on Iran's interests will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response.

items.headline: Homes lost, hungry babies: Nepal's mothers struggle in shelters
items.gist: Nepal's August 26 flash floods separated Sharmila Shrestha from her 14-month-old daughter for two or three days and destroyed her home; reunited at a crowded Kathmandu shelter, she can only feed her toddler the same heavy adult food as other evacuees because no baby food is available. The UNFPA estimates around 4,430 pregnant women are living across 15 municipalities in three flood-affected districts based on an affected population of about 310,000, with roughly 492 births expected in the following month and about 74 women potentially requiring emergency obstetric care.

items.headline: Nepal urges countries to limit travel advisories
items.gist: Nepal has urged friendly countries to confine travel advisories to specific flood-affected areas, highlighting that the rest of the country remains open and safe for travel and tourism. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Sunday that it and Nepal's missions abroad were working closely with friendly countries on the issue, after the United States issued a September 4 advisory placing Nepal under Level 2 "Exercise increased caution" due to natural disasters.

items.headline: UN names Nov 27 as day against child marriage
items.gist: The 193-member UN General Assembly on Friday adopted by consensus a resolution proclaiming November 27 every year as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, led by Sierra Leone with India among co-sponsors. The date marks the November 27, 2024 launch of India's 'Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat' campaign aiming to reduce child marriage prevalence by 10% by 2026 and make India child-marriage free by 2030, an initiative also championed by Sierra Leone's First Lady Fatima Maada Bio and Just Rights for Children Founder Bhuwan Ribhu.

items.headline: Moscow not ruling out trilateral Russia, US, China meeting
items.gist: Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on Sunday that Moscow has not ruled out a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Russia, the US and China, but that the main question is how the meeting's substance and expected results would be formulated. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov had earlier raised the possibility of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meeting at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November; Ushakov said on Sunday such a meeting would not be without merit but its organisation is the prerogative of the summit hosts.

items.headline: Germany 'wants war again': Russia on drone accusations
items.gist: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Germany "wants war again" in an interview published Sunday, dismissing Berlin's accusation that Russia sent low-level agents for an attempted hybrid attack involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport. Moscow and Berlin closed each other's cultural centres this week, with Lavrov accusing Germany of Nazism and saying the Russian leadership will draw appropriate conclusions; Germany, a main Ukraine ally, blamed Moscow for the incident at the strategic eastern airport.

items.headline: Lebanon president calls for US help as Israeli strikes kill 7
items.gist: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun urged Washington and the international community to help stop Israeli attacks that killed at least seven people on Sunday despite a truce and framework deal aimed at halting violence. Israel said it targeted Hezbollah operatives and sites in response to a drone attack on its troops near a strategic south Lebanon ridge; Aoun called Sunday's strikes, which damaged government premises and destroyed an out-of-service hospital, a dangerous escalation reaching Lebanese state institutions and health facilities.

items.headline: Trump admin makes another appeal over mail ballot curbs
items.gist: The Trump administration on Sunday renewed its appeal to the Supreme Court after US District Court Judge Indira Talwani extended an order blocking the Postal Service from enforcing President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail ballots ahead of the midterms. Solicitor General John Sauer said ballots have already begun mailing in North Carolina and more states will follow while the injunction remains, marking the third time the administration has asked the high court to intervene.

items.headline: Prince Harry's surprise UK return renews security row
items.gist: Prince Harry's return to Britain with wife Meghan and their two young children has reignited debate over whether taxpayers should fund their protection, with experts warning genuine threats likely exist. Harry, who quit royal duties in 2020 and lost a legal battle to retain UK taxpayer-funded security while living in California, has reportedly been pushing for reinstated police protection; when the family landed at Birmingham Airport on August 26 they had private security rather than police officers, according to British media.

items.headline: FIFA confirms Infantino will run in presidential election
items.gist: Gianni Infantino will stand in March's FIFA presidential election despite backlash over his now-abandoned plan to bring private investment into the World Cup, the global governing body confirmed on Sunday. A FIFA spokesperson said the president announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027; Infantino had declined to answer questions about his future as he arrived for the opening of the women's U-20 World Cup in Poland.

items.headline: Indonesia cancels flights as volcano erupts
items.gist: Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday for 30 seconds at 3:53 a.m., prompting cancellation of all flights at Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport as volcanic ash drifted across western Indonesia. Indonesia's Geological Agency said the Sunda Strait island had shown activity since Friday; no casualties or evacuation order was issued, though residents and visitors were warned to stay at least 3 kilometres from the active crater, with the nearest settlement more than 16 kilometres away.

items.headline: Putin, US envoys revive peace talks
items.gist: Russian President Vladimir Putin met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin on Saturday for more than three hours of closed-door talks to revive a stalled push to end the Russia-Ukraine war, with both sides agreeing to pause strikes on each other's capitals during the discussions. Putin ordered no strikes against Kyiv for three days from midnight, and Zelenskyy said Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Moscow through Monday; Washington's peace push has lost momentum as US attention has focused for six months on the Iran war, and the envoys were also due to visit Kyiv on Sunday.

items.headline: Wedding party fire in Congo leaves 22 dead
items.gist: A fire at a wedding party in Congo's capital Kinshasa left at least 22 people dead and several others injured, Lingwala regional mayor Norbert Mushunga said Saturday. The fire started Friday night and continued into early Saturday in a building in northern Kinshasa's Lingwala area, where narrow hallways were constricted by people trying to escape; several people, alive and dead, were laid by the roadside as attendees tried to help survivors.

items.headline: Iran strikes US ship in Strait of Hormuz
items.gist: Iran said Sunday it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, the latest salvo in a flare-up of fighting that began with US and Israeli attacks on Feb 28 and has persisted despite a June ceasefire announcement. The US did not immediately confirm the attack, which came a day after US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to a missile attack on Navy warships; at least five people were killed earlier in the week during a US bombardment of southern Iran, and the Trump administration is responding militarily while also targeting foreign financial institutions handling Iran's money.

items.headline: Fuel tanker explosion in Iran kills 11, injures 7
items.gist: A fuel tanker exploded in western Iran late Saturday, killing 11 people and injuring seven others near a traffic police station close to the Kurdish city of Sanandaj, some 400 kilometres west of Tehran, state media reported. IRNA said the tanker hit other cars before bursting into flames, citing a faulty brake system; the injured were transferred to hospitals, and experts blame Iran's high road fatality rate of more than 17,000 deaths annually on unsafe vehicles, disregard for traffic rules and inadequate emergency services.

items.headline: US ambassador calls violent Israeli settlers 'terrorists' after weeks of West Bank unrest
items.gist: US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee condemned Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, calling behaviour including squatting, burning cars, torching mosques and vandalising homes "an act of terror" during a visit to Turmus Ayya, which has reported frequent settler attacks. Such attacks have surged since the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, according to the UN humanitarian office; Huckabee also used the term "terrorists" last month after unrest in Qusra, and on Saturday referenced graffiti in Bazariya reading "Huckabee regards from the terrorists."

items.headline: Mudslide kills 3, leaves 10 missing in China
items.gist: A mudslide killed three people and left 10 missing in Suichuan County, Jiangxi province in eastern China, damaging a dozen houses after days of torrential rain from tropical cyclone Saudel, state media said Sunday. Rescuers relocated residents to safer ground; separately, CCTV reported two people killed in Hunan province from downpours, and Xinhua reported another person killed by a landslide in a different Jiangxi village a day earlier.

items.headline: Nepal floods: DNA testing offers last hope
items.gist: Amrit Diyali's family in Nepal is relying on DNA testing to identify whether a severed hand found downstream belongs to his younger brother Raj Kumar, missing with his wife and four-year-old son since devastating Aug 26 floods triggered by an avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border. Authorities are using DNA testing to identify hundreds of bodies recovered after the Bhotekoshi River floodwaters killed more than 1,300 and left around 5,000 missing, with police collecting 2,272 DNA samples—1,260 from bodies and 1,012 from relatives.

items.headline: South Korea pledges support for reconstruction
items.gist: Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal and South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun discussed ongoing search, rescue and relief operations following devastating floods that killed more than 1,300 and left around 5,000 missing, during a meeting in Kathmandu on Sunday. Khanal thanked South Korea for sending an inter-agency rapid response team, and the two held in-depth discussions on efforts to locate missing South Korean nationals.

Siraj explains that glaciers are dense ice bodies forming in cold regions where snow accumulates faster than it melts, hold about 69% of the world's freshwater, and cover roughly 10% of Earth's land; the Himalayan Hindu Kush region alone has an estimated 54,000 to 63,000 glaciers feeding at least 10 major Asian river systems. items.headline: Rajnath Singh set for 3-day Sri Lanka visit to boost defence ties
items.gist: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will visit Sri Lanka from September 8 to 10, the first visit by an Indian Defence Minister in 38 years since K.C. Pant in 1988, for talks with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, Prime Minister Harini Amarasuriya and Defence Secretary Sampath Thuyacontha on defence cooperation including air-defence systems and implementation of the April 5, 2025 India-Sri Lanka Defence Cooperation MoU.

items.headline: China teams scour ruins at flood-hit border crossing
items.gist: Chinese officials said on Sunday that workers recovered 12 more bodies as the search continued for hundreds still missing after a massive mudslide destroyed China's main border crossing with Nepal, opening devastated Gyirong County in Tibet to select media for the first time to show the scale of destruction at the destroyed immigration post. The mudslide has killed more than 1,300 people on both sides of the border with more than 5,000 missing; on the Chinese side 43 were confirmed dead and 519 remained missing as of Saturday, with recovery teams taking fingerprints and recording identifying features as families and diplomats privately expressed frustration over limited information-sharing.

items.headline: Bhutan leads Southeast Asia region in eliminating rabies
items.gist: Bhutan has become the first country in the WHO Southeast Asia region to eliminate dog-transmitted rabies as a public health problem, with WHO validating the achievement on Saturday and the kingdom's last rabies death recorded in June 2023. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus congratulated Bhutan as another step toward ending human deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030, crediting a two-pronged strategy of dog vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis, strong collaboration between health and agriculture ministries, and community engagement through De-suung volunteers.

items.gist: Skipper Ishan Kishan struck an unbeaten 111 (14 fours, 1 six) as East Zone reached 385 for four against South Zone on the opening day of the Duleep Trophy final in Chennai on Sunday, with Kumar Kushagra 63 not out and a fifth-wicket stand of 144 in 26.4 overs. items.headline: Antonelli dazzles to Italian GP victory
items.gist: Kimi Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix at Monza on Sunday with a charge from 19th on the grid—after exceeding permitted power-unit changes—to beat Mercedes teammate George Russell by 3.857 seconds, with Max Verstappen third, Lando Norris fourth, Oscar Piastri fifth and Lewis Hamilton sixth after Charles Leclerc crashed out triggering an early red flag. Antonelli's seventh win of the season and first home GP victory stretched his drivers' championship lead to 66 points over Russell (267 to 201), with Mercedes leading the constructors' standings on 468 points.

items.headline: Everton snatch a point off United
items.gist: Ainsley Maitland-Niles marked his Everton debut with a 96th-minute long-range equaliser to snatch a 2-2 draw against Manchester United, after Bryan Mbeumo had put United ahead early in the second half and substitute Benjamin Sesko's 88th-minute header looked to have won it. Tyrique George had levelled for Everton in the 83rd minute; the draw maintains Everton's unbeaten start and keeps them one point ahead of United, who have conceded twice in all three opening Premier League games.

items.headline: We plan together: Charani on India's spin strategy in Pak rout
items.gist: Young left-arm spinner Shree Charani, who took 3/7 as India bowled Pakistan out for their lowest-ever T20I total of 55 in a seven-wicket Women's T20 Asia Cup win in Dubai on Saturday, said slow bowlers map out strategy together before matches. Charani, Prema Rawat (3/9) and Deepti Sharma (2/5) combined to choke Pakistan's batting; India finished Group A on top with six points after winning all three games, and Charani is one wicket away from 50 T20I wickets.

items.headline: Italian GP: Gasly stuns Monza again with first-ever pole
items.gist: Alpine's Pierre Gasly claimed his first-ever Formula 1 pole position for the Italian Grand Prix at Monza on Saturday, finishing 0.060 seconds ahead of Mercedes' George Russell. Oscar Piastri was third-fastest but received a three-place grid penalty for impeding Red Bull's Liam Lawson in Q2, promoting Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton to the second row; championship leader Kimi Antonelli qualified seventh but starts at the back due to a planned engine change, while Gasly's 2020 Monza win remains his only F1 victory.

items.headline: I felt like I couldn't play tennis: Keys on her third-set implosion
items.gist: Madison Keys said she got off to a really good lead and then got scared and could not swing after squandering a 5-0 lead in the decider to crash out of the US Open. She felt Zheng Qinwen started playing better while she started playing poorly, adding that she felt like she could not play tennis anymore.

items.headline: Beyond recovery
items.gist: Ahead of World Physiotherapy Day on September 8, physiotherapy is increasingly moving beyond treating injuries to preventive care and rehabilitation across life stages, with specialists supporting cardiac recovery, women's health through pregnancy and postpartum, early intervention for children with developmental concerns, geriatric mobility, and sports injury prevention. Cardiovascular physiotherapist Dr Shraddha Patel emphasises heart and lung training after surgery, women's health physiotherapist Dr Sanjana Venkataraman highlights care from conception through childbirth, paediatric neuro physiotherapist Dr Aishwarya Talgeri stresses early milestone intervention, and sports physiotherapist Dr Vaibhavi Pathade notes more young people now seek physiotherapy before injury rather than only after.

items.headline: Monsoon barrier damage
items.gist: Excessive monsoon moisture, sweat, fungal growth and over-cleansing can disrupt the skin barrier, causing dryness, sensitivity, redness, breakouts, itching, rough texture and slow healing. Ayurvedic remedies suggested include aloe vera gel for hydration, rose water as a toner, oatmeal and honey masks, sandalwood paste with rose water, and turmeric with yogurt or honey, alongside lifestyle tips such as staying hydrated and eating antioxidant-rich seasonal fruits and vegetables.

items.headline: DHUMAPANA THERAPY OR TREND?
items.gist: Medicated Ayurvedic smoking, or Dhumapana—the controlled inhalation of smoke from specific medicinal herbs—gained attention after lifestyle creator Shenaz Treasury shared undergoing the physician-prescribed treatment at an Ayurveda clinic, though experts stress it differs from cigarette smoking. Dr Anjana Kalia and Dr Neeru Jain explain it is a traditional, supervised therapeutic procedure described in texts such as Charaka Samhita for head and upper respiratory disorders, but warn smoke and fine particles may irritate the respiratory tract, herbal cigarettes are not equivalent, and more clinical research is needed on benefits and long-term safety.

items.headline: KAKAPO — The fattest, heaviest, flightless Parrots
items.gist: The kakapo, the world's heaviest flightless parrot weighing up to 4 kilograms, is found in New Zealand's protected island sanctuaries and can live 60 to 90 years. Nearly extinct by the 1900s after predators such as cats and stoats were introduced, a Department of Conservation recovery programme launched in 1995 when only 51 remained has raised numbers to over 320; this year a bountiful rimu berry harvest prompted a record breeding season, with the youngest 2026 chick, female Awarua-A3, hatching on March 30.

items.headline: Rama answers Vaali
items.gist: A dying Vaali questions Rama's righteousness, his enmity with Vaali and why He had to kill him; Navalpakkam Vasudevachariar recounts that Rama answers every objection, telling Vaali he ignored conventions, failed to consult intellectual superiors and acted as he pleased. Rama says all earth—including animals, birds and trees—is under Ikshvaku control, that as Bharata's representative enforcing moral rule He must punish Vaali for misbehaving with Sugreeva's wife as with a daughter-in-law, and that He cannot spare one who has sinned and broken all rules.

items.headline: Balanced bond portfolio blueprint
items.gist: Vaishali R. Venkat outlines how to build a bond portfolio that can withstand defaults, changing interest rates and shifting economic conditions, starting with clarifying when and how much money is needed, desired income versus capital appreciation, and risk tolerance.
items.paragraph: Vaishali R. Venkat outlines how to build a bond portfolio that can withstand defaults, changing interest rates and shifting economic conditions, starting with clarifying when and how much money is needed, desired income versus capital appreciation, and risk tolerance. She advises mixing government securities, Treasury bonds, corporate bonds and bank bonds across issuers, sectors and maturities; scrutinising credit ratings without treating them as guarantees; and rebalancing at least every six months to a year while tracking RBI announcements, issuer developments and macro indicators such as GDP growth, inflation and CPI.

items.headline: Buying insurance at discount? Think twice
items.gist: K. Nitya Kalyani warns that in insurance the cheapest option is not necessarily the best value, because a lower premium often reflects a changed bundle of risks, conditions, exclusions and benefits rather than the same cover at a better price.
items.paragraph: K. Nitya Kalyani warns that in insurance the cheapest option is not necessarily the best value, because a lower premium often reflects a changed bundle of risks, conditions, exclusions and benefits rather than the same cover at a better price. She cites examples including a discounted motor policy restricting repairs to non-network garages, a home fire policy discount that removed flood cover before IRDAI mandated bundled flood cover from 2021, and windshield claims that can cost more in lost no-claim bonus than the repair itself, urging buyers to ask what add-ons, deductibles, co-pay, cashless restrictions or repairer limits have changed before accepting a discount.

items.headline: Scientists plan to find out if there is alien debris on the Moon
items.gist: A SETI Institute–led team proposes that microscopic particles shed by alien civilisations may have accumulated on the lunar surface, making the moon a possible archive of extraterrestrial technology. Modelling how such "Arkhipov particles" and operational "Bracewell particles" could reach the solar system, the researchers suggest a mission could sift about a cubic metre of lunar soil for artificial grains, though distinguishing alien debris from human spacecraft litter would require chemical analysis.

items.headline: Sulphuric acid: not so deadly
items.gist: Researchers report in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on September 4 that certain peptides remain stable for weeks at room temperature in 98% concentrated sulphuric acid and fold into omega-loop shapes, using acid molecules as scaffolding—a first for a biological macromolecule in that solvent, after earlier work on nucleic acid bases and amino acids. Because hydrolysis needs water, the near-waterless acid does not break peptide bonds; the findings challenge assumptions that Venus’s sulphuric-acid clouds are too harsh for complex chemistry relevant to the search for life beyond Earth.

items.headline: Proposed Karnataka AI University to begin skill programmes before full-fledged campus takes shape
items.gist: Karnataka plans to start AI education and skill-development initiatives before the proposed Karnataka Artificial Intelligence University is fully operational, with the advisory committee’s first meeting in Bengaluru on Saturday under Infosys co-founder Kris Gopalakrishnan and IT-BT and Science and Technology Department secretary Dr N Manjula as co-chair discussing certificate, diploma, reskilling and executive education programmes. Programmes will focus on generative and agentic AI, data analytics, cloud computing, cybersecurity, AI infrastructure and data centres, physical AI, semiconductor and hardware applications, and AI literacy, targeting university students and graduates, working technology professionals, other-sector professionals, and rural youth.

items.headline: No 'space' for job loss, say ISRO staff amid privatisation moves
items.gist: Two days after the Indian Space Research Organisation's Staff Association wrote to chairperson V Narayanan expressing concerns over the organisation's privatisation plans, members clarified they are not against private players entering the space industry but want ISRO to clearly communicate its future direction to employees. On 6 September an office bearer told The Print that if the government outsources tasks such as rocket building and technology development to private companies, staff need clarity on ISRO's role; on 4 September the association sent a five-page letter citing IN-SPACe chairperson Pawan Goenka's comments that ISRO will no longer make or manufacture launch vehicles, work that will go to the private sector or PSUs.
items.paragraph: Two days after the Indian Space Research Organisation's Staff Association wrote to chairperson V Narayanan expressing concerns over the organisation's privatisation plans, members clarified they are not against private players entering the space industry but want ISRO to clearly communicate its future direction to employees. With no official communication on transferring launch vehicle design and manufacturing, a VSSC office bearer said at least 50 per cent of the workforce could lose jobs if the private sector takes over, though employees are not completely hostile to privatisation if integration preserves the relevance of existing staff and centres.

items.headline: ISRO's role is by no means diminishing: space officials
items.gist: IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Kumar Goenka and ISRO refuted suggestions that privatisation threatens ISRO's workforce, responding to a September 4 joint letter from nine ISRO employee associations citing Goenka's August 21 remarks that ISRO would eventually not make or manufacture launch vehicles. Goenka said ISRO's role is "by no means diminishing" and it will remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector, concentrating on advanced R&D, scientific and strategic missions and infrastructure including the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035 and a crewed lunar mission by 2040, while industry scales mature launch vehicles and satellites; ISRO called privatisation suggestions "completely baseless and incorrect."

items.gist: ISRO clarified on Sunday it would neither be privatised nor diminished, saying private-sector participation lets it focus on frontier R&D, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems and deep-space missions while industry scales mature technologies. items.headline: 'India must look beyond unicorns to measure startup success'
items.gist: KPMG India Partner Akhilesh Tuteja told DH that India's startup ecosystem is diffusing innovation beyond consumer apps into agriculture, energy, smart manufacturing and space, while investor attention is shifting toward AI, semiconductors, infrastructure and industry-specific applications with greater scrutiny of profitability and burn rates. items.headline: Sharpest pictures of sun’s surface reveal previously unseen whirlpools
items.gist: Scientists using the NSF Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) in Hawaii—the world’s largest solar telescope, with a four-metre primary mirror—have captured the highest-resolution images yet of the sun’s photosphere, revealing small plasma coils at granule edges and fast-spinning vortices that grow up to 2.7 times their size in 18 seconds and rotate at 1.6–2.8 km/s.
items.paragraph: Scientists using the NSF Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) in Hawaii—the world’s largest solar telescope, with a four-metre primary mirror—have captured the highest-resolution images yet of the sun’s photosphere, revealing small plasma coils at granule edges and fast-spinning vortices that grow up to 2.7 times their size in 18 seconds and rotate at 1.6–2.8 km/s. Published in Nature on August 5, the findings suggest these whirlpools efficiently transport energy and magnetic flux, braid magnetic fields at small scales, and may help explain solar flares and the unexpectedly hot outer atmosphere.

items.headline: Studies show glaciers are shrinking
items.gist: Nazeer Waris writes that mounting evidence shows global glaciers are shrinking as warming accelerates melting beyond natural rates. NASA GRACE satellite data from 2002 to 2020 shows Antarctica lost around 150 gigatons of ice annually, contributing 0.4 millimetres of global sea-level rise per year; ice caps in the Canadian Arctic have shrunk 50% in the last century, and ICIMOD's March 2026 Hindu Kush Himalaya Glacier Outlook found ice loss rates across the region have doubled since 2000 despite dangerously under-researched coverage of only around 38 glaciers with long-term monitoring on 21.

items.headline: Frontier professionals: The new AI-first force that redesigns work
items.gist: Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index finds one in three Indian workers are "frontier professionals" who redesign multi-step workflows around AI agents, the highest share globally at 16%, with 78% of India's AI users saying AI enables work that was impossible a year ago. Industry leaders say these workers combine AI fluency, domain expertise and human judgement to drive productivity gains and typically command premium salaries as organisations move from experimentation to practical adoption.

items.headline: Why Australia's music industry banned AI music in chart listing
items.gist: Sahana Venugopal reports that on August 25 Australia’s ARIA barred wholly AI-generated songs from its charts while allowing recordings that are “substantially human made,” after an undisclosed AI remix of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” by Josh Fawaz ranked second on ARIA’s top 20 Australian singles chart and drew over 23 million YouTube views. The piece notes ARIA may reject or remove ineligible tracks from charts and awards, that publishers are suing AI platforms over copyrighted training data—including a landmark $1.5 billion Anthropic settlement—and that Spotify will soon label “AI Persona” artists as listeners demand clearer differentiation and filtering of AI-assisted music.

items.headline: Lines on a map won't resolve India-China conflict (Opinion)
items.gist: Praveen Swami argues that speculation after the meeting between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi about an interim border agreement misses that the China-India border conflict has never been about the few dozen kilometres separating their claim-lines. He recounts how Beijing's 1962 use of force along the Line of Control was meant to send a message to New Delhi, Taiwan, the US and the Soviet Union amid PLA concerns over Xinjiang insurgency, CIA support to Tibetan and Kazakh rebels, and Indian asylum to secessionists including Yulbars Khan after 1951.

items.headline: 'Govt at doorstep' welcome (Opinion)
items.gist: Raghuram S of Bengaluru welcomes the state government's launch of Praja Seva services to reach citizens at their doorstep with government schemes and welfare measures, saying those left out especially in remote villages and districts will now be able to participate in the state's governance and welfare development schedule. He says if implemented with honesty the initiative can help genuine needy people, but dedication on the part of officials is absolutely needed for it to work for Karnataka and its people.

items.headline: When childhood is no longer safe (Opinion)
items.gist: The piece cites chilling Delhi-NCR cases including a three-year-old girl allegedly sexually assaulted by a school bus driver in Bawana and a 16-year-old student allegedly gang-raped inside a moving sleeper bus after boarding at Greater Noida, arguing India is failing children and women in their basic right to live without fear. It says sexual violence is a national social emergency, calls for rigorous police verification, psychological screening and periodic re-verification of school transport staff, functioning CCTV, GPS and panic buttons on school buses, and suspension rather than merely fines for private buses with safety violations.

items.headline: What does Teachers' Day mean? (Opinion)
items.gist: The article questions whether Teachers' Day on September 5 truly recognises teachers or merely glorifies them for one day, noting teachers today are expected to be educators, mentors, counsellors, administrators, technology experts and more while also handling absentee follow-ups, government programmes, elections, census activities, surveys and awareness campaigns. It argues genuine respect means valuing teachers' time, professional expertise, intellectual freedom and right to focus on teaching and learning, and that teachers should not become responsible for every task simply because the system needs someone to perform it.

items.headline: The political cost of UCT schemes (Opinion)
items.gist: K.R. Shanmugam argues that unconditional cash transfer schemes such as Tamil Nadu's Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thittam, despite costing States about $18 billion in 2025-26, can impose political costs through inclusion and exclusion errors—illustrated by the Tamil Nadu scheme covering 1.13 crore women and later adding 16.94 lakh more after complaints, at ₹13,807 crore in 2025-26—and that conditional transfers tied to education or other outcomes may carry lower political risk.

items.headline: India's unemployment data dilemma (Opinion)
items.gist: Santosh V. Perumal writes that India's new monthly PLFS unemployment rate—5.1% in July, a four-month low—reflects seasonal agricultural hiring rather than structural improvement in a labour market where about 90% work informally; household inflation expectations remain about four percentage points above RBI projections, limiting the payoff from inflation targeting when the Phillips curve appears flat.

items.headline: Why India should keep its SCO seat (Opinion)
items.gist: Vanshika Saraf argues India should retain its Shanghai Cooperation Organisation membership despite underwhelming outcomes and difficult relationships with China and Pakistan, because geography ties India's interests to Central Asia, full membership gives consensus-blocking agency—as shown by refusing Belt and Road endorsement—and the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure offers a platform on Afghanistan, extremism and narcotics routes India cannot ignore.

items.headline: RERA toothless (Opinion)
items.gist: N Sadhasiva Reddy of Bengaluru writes that the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, promised as a game-changer for homebuyers, has become a toothless tiger because authorities issue refund and compensation orders that local revenue departments fail to execute, builders exploit insolvency proceedings under the IBC to freeze RERA orders, and buyers remain trapped between EMIs and legal fees without direct penal powers or strict enforcement.

items.headline: A look that killed the noise (Opinion)
items.gist: Prakash Jothady recalls Bengaluru schooldays when teachers needed no technology beyond a single stern look to silence classrooms, arguing those simpler blackboard classrooms taught punctuality, discipline and responsibility through encouragement, appreciation and firm correction—and that on Teachers' Day he remembers educators for shaping character, not gadgets.

items.headline: What good is a title without better working conditions? (Opinion)
items.gist: C V Aravind of Bengaluru writes that Karnataka CM D K Shivakumar's permission for teachers to use the 'Tr' prefix is a cosmetic sop, and that teachers instead need better working conditions, improved salaries, promotional avenues and higher pensions rather than stepmotherly treatment of a noble profession.

items.headline: Juvenile justice faces Section 15 test (Opinion)
items.gist: Advocate Geeta Sajjanshetty and social worker Sangappa Vaggar argue the Supreme Court's adult-trial ruling for a 16-year-old accused of murder highlights Section 15's flawed design—assessing capacity presumes guilt, age correlates poorly with maturity, assessments vary widely without standardised protocols, and children's courts often ignore mandatory Section 19 reviews—calling on Parliament to devise a scientifically validated, rights-based framework instead of retribution.

items.headline: Payout farce exposes NCLT's flawed process (Opinion)
items.gist: An editorial criticises the NCLT special bench's stay on approving a Rs 6.25 crore payout plan against over Rs 22,006.57 crore in claims against Essel group founder Subhash Chandra—a 99.97% haircut—after public outrage, noting 80.81% voting support included 61.78% from associates and questioning declared net worth figures ranging from Rs 31.79 crore to Rs 45,888 crore while ordinary guarantors face harsher recovery action.

items.headline: A Ganesh Chaturthi without PoP pollution (Opinion)
items.gist: An editorial urges ecofriendly Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations, supporting Karnataka's push against Plaster of Paris and chemical-coloured idols and strict high court enforcement because PoP and toxic paints harm water bodies, while warning that loud DJ systems, route disputes and provocative processions—as seen in Nagamangala (2024) and Maddur (2025)—can turn festivity into law-and-order crises; organisers should follow police routes, sound limits and timings so faith and environmental and public peace coexist.

items.headline: A conversation is much more than words (Opinion)
items.gist: The writer recounts a family argument over a current event in which she spoke from feeling, her brother from reason and her sister from wider social implications, each using a different "language" of truth. She argues that before consequential discussions, people should recognise whether the exchange is emotional, logical or social, and respond in the language being spoken so empathy, coherence and perspective are not lost in translation.

items.headline: From Ambedkar to Rahul Gandhi—the unfinished fight against Manu (Opinion)
items.gist: The writer traces how B R Ambedkar's 1951 critique of Manusmriti, especially its subordination of women under male guardianship, fed into his battle for the Hindu Code Bill and resignation from the Cabinet when reform stalled before enactment in 1955–56. Rahul Gandhi's 2026 Pune call to "smash the patriarchy" echoes that unfinished struggle, but the piece argues it must move beyond slogans to concrete legal measures against digital sexual abuse, doxxing, deepfake pornography and threats targeting women in public life.

items.headline: Why you need a financial advisor even more now? (Opinion)
items.gist: Mrin Agarwal argues that exiting underperforming equity funds during weak phases often causes investors to miss subsequent recovery, creating a vicious cycle of chasing recent winners. Using the example of Anurag, who lacked adequate medical cover and held an illiquid, underperforming portfolio heavy in smallcap funds, she contends advisors deliver value through comprehensive planning, discipline during volatility, debt repayment strategy, international education savings, and tax filing support—not merely scheme selection.

items.headline: Does inflation targeting work in India? (Opinion)
items.gist: Rohit Azad and Indranil Chowdhury argue that after a decade of RBI inflation targeting aimed at 4% within a ±2 percentage-point band, India’s New Keynesian Phillips curve appears flat in monthly IIP and CPI data from April 2012 to March 2026, while household inflation expectations in RBI surveys consistently exceed projections by about four percentage points. They contend that with roughly 92% of workers lacking bargaining power, raising repo rates can lower output and employment without commensurate inflation gains—the opposite of what the framework assumes.
